events.text: Dark, and warm, and close. Four small bodies push at you from every side, and every one of them smells of milk and of you. Above the dark there is soil, and above the soil, a long way up, something old and quiet that the earth itself seems to keep its voice down for. Pine roots hang through the ceiling like the fingers of a sleeper.

choices.text: Push your way into the warm middle of the pile

effects.log: You burrow, you shove, you climb over a sibling who complains in a voice like a squeaking hinge. The middle is warmest. You sleep there, and you will spend a whole life finding the middle of things.

choices.text: Crawl toward the cold that comes from one side

effects.log: The cold has a smell: frost, wet grass, smoke from somewhere far, a dog. The world. You lie with your nose in it until a bigger, warmer shape picks you up by the scruff and puts you back.

choices.text: Lie still and listen to the quiet above

effects.log: It is not a sound. It is the shape of a sound that stopped a hundred years ago. You listen to it until you sleep, and in your sleep it is almost a voice, and almost kind.

events.text: Your eyes are open now. The mourners come up the hill on the full moon of the eighth month: a family in white, with sickles to cut the grass on the mound and a cloth bundle of rice cakes steamed on pine needles. They bow on the grass over your head. Through the soil you hear them talk about a grandfather who liked his drink, and laugh, and then cry a little. When they go, the rice cakes are still on the mound.

choices.text: Wait for your mother to fetch one down

effects.log: She brings down a half-moon rice cake still smelling of pine, and you all fight over it. Sesame and honey inside. The dead grandfather, you decide, was a generous man.

choices.text: Creep out and take one yourself

effects.log: Out of the earth for the first time, under a moon as big as the sky. You take the smallest cake and run back so fast you fall in head first. Your mother looks at you with her ears flat and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Listen to the family until the last voice is gone

effects.log: They talk about him for a long time: his laugh, his bad knee, a song he sang wrong every year. You do not understand a word yet. You understand the sound. It is the sound of people who miss someone.

events.text: The smallest of the five was always the last to the milk and the first to the entrance, nose up, wanting the night. One dusk it goes out alone onto the grass of the mound. A shape drops out of the pine with no sound at all, and is gone again, and so is the smallest. Your mother comes back at moonrise and counts with her nose, once, twice, and then lies across the entrance all night and does not sleep.

choices.text: Lie across the entrance with her

effects.log: All night, your small back against her large one, both of you watching the pine. Nothing comes. In the morning she licks your face once, hard, as if to make sure it is still there.

choices.text: Learn the owl's hour

effects.log: Dusk and the hour before dawn, when the light is grey and nothing has a shadow. You will never in your life cross open grass at the owl's hour. It is the first rule you make yourself.

choices.text: Go out onto the mound and look at the pine

effects.log: You stand on the grass where the smallest stood and stare up at the dark branches until your mother drags you in by the scruff. It hurts. You are glad it hurts. (-3 health)

events.text: Men with sickles again, but not at the full moon and not in white: the family has hired two labourers to cut the grass on all the old mounds, and one of them stops at yours. "Fox hole," he says, and pokes the entrance with the handle. "Want me to smoke it out?" The other spits. "Leave it. A fox in a grave keeps the grave lucky. Everybody knows that." Nobody knows that. You hold very still in the dark.

choices.text: Stay still until they go

effects.log: They argue about luck for a while and go on to the next mound. That evening a bowl of millet is set by the entrance, very carefully, by somebody who will tell everybody it was not them.

choices.text: Leave the earth that night and find another

effects.log: You go out under the moon with your littermates and find a bank of red soil above the paddies. It is not home. Nothing is ever home again quite the way the first earth was.

choices.text: Show yourself at the entrance, small and fierce

effects.log: You put your head out and bare every tooth you have. The labourer laughs so hard he sits down. "There," says the other. "It is lucky. Look at it." They leave the mound uncut on one side, which is your side.

events.text: Decades on, the mound is still there, rounder and lower. The family still comes up on the full moon of the eighth month, but it is the grandchildren now, with sickles, and a little one who has been told about the fox in the grave and wants very much to see it. The rice cakes are left, as always. One of them has been set a little apart, by the entrance, on a clean leaf.

choices.text: Take the cake on the leaf, and leave the others

effects.log: You take the one meant for you and leave the dead their share. The next year there are two on the leaf. You do not know which of them started it. It does not matter.

choices.text: Let the little one see you, once, at the edge of the pines

effects.log: One glimpse: a red-brown fox at the edge of the pines, looking back. The little one shrieks with joy. In the village they say the family on the hill has a lucky grave, and they are right.

choices.text: Stay down in the dark and let them be

effects.log: You listen to them through the soil, the way you did when you were blind: a new song sung wrong, a new grandfather missed. People do not change much. You find you are glad.

events.text: Your mother teaches with her teeth. She takes you to the edge of the pines above the village and makes you lie in the grass while a dog goes by on the path below, nose down. "The first rule," she says, in the small sounds foxes use. "Never let a dog smell you twice. Once, it is a fox. Twice, it is you."

choices.text: Lie still until the dog is gone

effects.log: The dog stops, sniffs the air, sneezes, and goes on. Your heart is beating so hard you think the whole village can hear it. "Good," says your mother. That is all. It is enough.

choices.text: Ask why twice is worse than once

effects.log: "Because a dog remembers," she says, "and a dog has a master, and a master has a bow. Once is an accident. Twice is a hunt." You never forget it.

choices.text: Creep closer to smell the dog yourself

effects.log: You get close enough to smell it: wet fur, millet, smoke. Then it smells you, and your mother has you by the scruff and over the bank before the first bark. That night she does not let you sleep in the warm middle. (-3 health)

events.text: Dusk on the hill road. A man comes up it with a wooden A-frame on his back, loaded with straw bags, and a forked stick in his hand to prop the frame when he rests. Your mother goes flat in the grass so fast you do not see her move. "The second rule," she says, when he is gone. "Never cross a salt peddler. Not on the road, not in a yard, not in your dreams."

choices.text: Ask what is in the bags

effects.log: "Salt, from the pans by the sea, boiled out over fires all summer," she says. "They carry the fire with them. They see what we are." You do not understand. You will.

choices.text: Watch the way he walks

effects.log: He walks like a man who is never in a hurry and never lost. Every few steps he looks at the verge, at the long grass, at the shadows. He is not looking for anything. He is just looking.

choices.text: Ask if a salt peddler has ever caught a fox

effects.log: Your mother does not answer for a long time. Then she says, "Your grandmother's sister," and nothing more, and you walk home behind her in a silence like snow.

events.text: A full moon. Your mother sits on the grave mound with her face turned up, breathing slowly, and when she opens her mouth to yawn you see it: a point of pale light behind her teeth, no bigger than a grain of rice, that comes and goes with her breath. "The third rule," she says, and closes her mouth on it. "Never let your bead into another mouth. Not to help. Not for love. Not ever."

choices.text: Ask what a bead is

effects.log: "The moon, kept," she says. "A hundred years of full moons, kept in the mouth. It is the only thing a fox owns." You go to sleep thinking about owning the moon.

choices.text: Ask what happens if it goes into another mouth

effects.log: "Then they have it," she says, "and they look at the earth, or at the sky, and know things. And you are a fox again, only a fox, and old." She says it as if she had seen it. Perhaps she has.

choices.text: Sit beside her and turn your face to the moon

effects.log: You sit as she sits and breathe as she breathes, and nothing happens, and nothing happens, and the moon goes over. "Not yet," she says. "Not for many years. But you sat. That is the beginning."

events.text: Lamplight from a farmhouse falls across the yard, and your mother crosses the edge of it on her way back from the hen-house. For one step her shadow goes long across the paper door, and it has two tails. Then she is past, and it has one. She sees you looking. She does not stop walking.

choices.text: Ask her about the second tail

effects.log: "What tail?" she says. You ask again. She looks at you for a long time. "Every tail is one more thing to hide," she says. "Count your own, when you have them. Never count mine."

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep it like she does

effects.log: You never mention it. Some nights, when she thinks you are asleep, she lets the second tail lie over all of you like a blanket. You are not asleep.

choices.text: Try to make your own shadow grow a tail in the lamplight

effects.log: You walk back and forth across the edge of the light until the farm dog starts up. One tail. One small, ordinary tail. Your mother carries you home by the scruff, which is how she laughs.

events.text: One autumn night your mother goes down to the paddies and does not come back. Not by dawn. Not by the next night. On the third day you follow her scent down the hill. It goes along the dyke, across the stream, up onto the hill road, and stops in the middle of the road, the way a fox's track stops when it stands up on two feet and walks on as something else.

choices.text: Follow the road toward the village

effects.log: At the edge of the village there is a stranger sweeping a yard, in a plain cotton jacket, who looks up at the hill as you watch, and then away, and goes inside. You never see that face again. You never stop looking for it.

choices.text: Go back to the earth and wait

effects.log: You wait all winter. The littermates leave one by one. In spring you understand that waiting is also an answer, and stop. (-4 health)

choices.text: Lie down where the track ends, and remember her rules

effects.log: A dog twice. A salt peddler. The bead. You say them over in the small sounds until the frost comes. Then you get up and go back to the hill, a fox on your own.

events.text: Four of you now. The boldest is a red vixen, redder than any of you, who bites first and asks nothing: you call her Ember. The one who hides from the moon you call Moon-Shy. The one with two white forepaws, as if it had stepped in snow, is White-Paw. And the quiet one who goes where you go, always a step behind, is Shadow. Every night the pile sorts itself, and somebody sleeps beside you.

choices.text: Sleep beside Ember

effects.log: Ember sleeps like a fight. She kicks, she bites in her sleep, she wakes you to ask if you can smell the hen-house. You can. She grins. You will never be bored.

choices.text: Sleep beside Shadow

effects.log: Shadow tucks its nose under your chin and does not move all night. In the morning it is still there, watching you wake, as if making sure you were real.

choices.text: Sleep beside White-Paw

effects.log: White-Paw is soft and patient and smells faintly of snow even in summer. It washes your ears without being asked. Of all of you, it is the one people will want.

events.text: Moon-Shy will not come out on full-moon nights. The others go down to the paddies and Moon-Shy lies at the back of the earth with its eyes shut, trembling, as if the moon were a dog. "It looks at me," Moon-Shy says. "It looks right into me."

choices.text: Take Moon-Shy up onto the mound at moonrise

ok.log: You sit on the grass with Moon-Shy pressed against you, and the moon comes up, and looks, and Moon-Shy looks back. "Oh," it says. "It is only looking." It is the bravest thing you have seen a fox do.

fail.log: Moon-Shy gets as far as the entrance and turns back. You stay out alone for a while so it will not feel watched. It is a kindness, of a sort.

choices.text: Stay in with Moon-Shy on the full-moon nights

effects.log: You lie together in the dark and tell each other what the moon must look like tonight, and make it worse and worse until you are both laughing. It is not courage. It is company, which is nearly as useful.

choices.text: Tell Moon-Shy the moon is the only thing a fox can own

effects.log: Moon-Shy thinks about it for a whole month. At the next full moon it comes out, alone, and sits on the very edge of the mound with its back to the moon. It is a start.

events.text: Ember comes back from a night in the rich house's yard below the hill smelling of warm floors and sesame oil. "They have a room with a fire under it," she says. "They put rice in bowls with lids. They had a daughter who died, and the mother still talks to her at night." Her eyes are very bright. "Somebody should be their daughter. They would not even have to know."

choices.text: Tell her it is the most dangerous thing you ever heard

effects.log: "Dangerous for them," Ember says, "or for me?" She does not wait for the answer. She goes back to the yard the next night, and the next, and comes home later every time.

choices.text: Go down with her and look

effects.log: Through a gap in the fence: a lit paper door, a woman's shadow, a voice talking softly to nobody. Ember watches it like a starving thing watches a hen. You pull her away. You are not sure, after, which of you wanted to stay.

choices.text: Ask her what she would do with a fire under the floor

effects.log: "Lie on it," Ember says at once. "All winter. And be called something. Not Ember. A name with a family in it." She says it so seriously that you do not laugh.

events.text: The earth is too small for grown foxes. Moon-Shy goes first, east, toward the hills with no villages. Ember goes down toward the rich house and does not look back. White-Paw goes north along the stream. Shadow sits at the entrance and waits to see which way you will go.

choices.text: Let Shadow come with you

effects.log: You go up toward the old graves on the ridge, and Shadow goes a step behind you, the way it always has. Two foxes on one hill is one too many, the old foxes say. The old foxes have never had a Shadow.

choices.text: Send Shadow its own way, for its own sake

effects.log: You growl it off, twice, and the second time it goes, down to the reed beds, looking back. It is the right thing for a fox. You lie awake for a month knowing it was right.

choices.text: Go after Ember instead

effects.log: You follow Ember's scent to the rich house's fence and stop there. She is inside somewhere. You can smell the fire under the floor. You go home alone, and Shadow is waiting at the entrance, and you are glad.

events.text: Shadow is grey at the muzzle now, and slow on the dyke, and sleeps most of the day. It has no bead. It never sat on the mound at the full moon; it only sat beside you. Many winters, a long life for a field fox. You have had as many, and you are not grey at all, and Shadow has noticed.

choices.text: Stay with Shadow through the last winter

effects.log: You bring it voles it cannot catch and lie against it when the frost comes. One morning it does not wake. You bury it in the bank above the paddies, the way people bury their own, and sit there until dark. (-4 health)

choices.text: Try to share the moon with it

effects.log: You sit with your mouth against its ear on the full-moon night and breathe out everything the moon gave you. It is not enough. Nothing is. But Shadow lives till spring, and sees the swallows come back.

choices.text: Ask Shadow why it followed you all its life

effects.log: "You were going somewhere," Shadow says. "Everyone else was only going." It dies in the spring. You go somewhere, after, because it would be rude not to.

events.text: The farmhouse at the end of the dyke keeps a broody hen in a straw basket on the porch. She is fat and warm and asleep on twelve eggs, and you want her more than you have ever wanted anything. Under the eaves above her, in a nest of mud and straw, a swallow is not asleep. It watches you come over the wall.

choices.text: Go for the hen anyway

ok.log: The swallow shrieks, the dog wakes, the house wakes, and you are over the wall with a mouthful of hen and a farmer's shoe flying after you. Delicious. Terrifying. You will remember the swallow.

fail.log: The swallow shrieks before you are halfway across the yard. The whole house is up. You leave with nothing but the farmer's shoe, which hit you. (-5 health)

choices.text: Back over the wall, and watch the swallow from the persimmon tree

effects.log: It watches you all night, from the nest, and you watch it, from the tree. At dawn it goes out after insects and comes back and looks at you again, as if to say: still here?

choices.text: Try to slip past the swallow's side of the yard

effects.log: There is no side of the yard the swallow cannot see. It shrieks. You go. The hen sleeps through all of it.

events.text: The swallow knows you. Not as a fox: as you. You come over the wall on a night with no moon, low and quiet, a shadow among shadows, and the swallow puts its head out of the nest and shrieks as if you were standing in lamplight with your name on a banner. The farmer's wife comes out with a broom. "That bird," she says to her husband, "sees the things we can't."

choices.text: Lie flat in the shadow of the jar platform

effects.log: The broom goes past two hands from your nose. The farmer's wife looks at the dark for a long time, then at the swallow, then goes in and bars the door. The swallow keeps watching you until dawn.

choices.text: Look up at the swallow, and let it look at you

effects.log: Some things see what you are. Dogs. Salt peddlers. A swallow under the eaves. It is not angry. It is simply not going to let you have the hen. You find you respect it.

choices.text: Leave, and come back on a rainy night when swallows sleep

effects.log: Swallows do not sleep on rainy nights. Swallows, it turns out, do not sleep on any night when you are in the yard.

events.text: A night of wind. The swallow's nest has cracked and come half away from the eaves, and the swallow sits on the edge of it over four chicks, unable to leave them, unable to shriek loud enough over the wind. The hen is asleep. The dog is asleep. You could take the hen, and the nest too, and nobody in the world would know.

choices.text: Take nothing, and go

effects.log: You stand in the yard for a long time with the wind in your fur. Then you go back over the wall, hungry. In the morning the farmer finds the cracked nest and props it up with a board, and never knows how lucky the whole yard was.

choices.text: Take the hen only

effects.log: You take the hen and leave the nest. On the way over the wall you look back. The swallow is watching you, and does not make a sound. That is worse than the shriek.

choices.text: Take both

effects.log: A full belly. In the spring no swallow comes back to the eaves of that house, and the farmer's wife says the luck has gone out of it. She is right, though she is wrong about why.

events.text: Spring, and the swallows come back to the eaves of the farmhouse from wherever swallows go. One of this year's chicks has fallen out of the nest into the yard, with a leg bent wrong, and is crying. The farmer's children are in the fields. The cat from the next house is on the wall.

choices.text: Pick the chick up in your mouth, gently, and put it on the porch

ok.log: Soft as an egg in your teeth. You set it on the porch where the children will find it, and go. In the evening a child binds its leg with a thread. The old swallow under the eaves watches you go over the wall, and does not shriek.

fail.log: The farmer's wife comes out at exactly the wrong moment and sees a fox with a chick in its mouth. Her scream is legendary. The chick lives: she makes sure of it. Your name in that yard does not.

choices.text: Chase the cat off the wall

effects.log: The cat goes. The chick cries in the yard until the children come home and find it. The swallow under the eaves saw who chased the cat. Swallows remember, the way dogs do, only kinder.

choices.text: It is a swallow. Leave it

effects.log: You go back to the dyke. That evening, from the hill, you hear the children find it and shout. Somebody else's luck. Not yours.

events.text: The household at the foot of the east ridge hunts. Their dogs are not yard dogs: a brindle hound with a torn ear and a yellow dog with a voice like a temple bell, kept lean, fed after the hunt. Their master carries a short bow and pays the village boys a coin for every fox earth they show him. This morning the brindle stopped on the dyke where you crossed at midnight, and put her nose down, and kept it there.

choices.text: Lay a false trail along the stream and back

effects.log: Through the water, out on the far bank, round the willow, back into the water. The brindle loses it at the willow. She will not lose it the next time. You know that, and so does she.

choices.text: Lie up in the reed beds and watch them work

effects.log: All afternoon you watch them quarter the stubble: the brindle low and silent, the yellow dog loud and behind. The brindle is the one to fear. The yellow dog only tells everyone where the brindle is.

choices.text: Move to another hill for a season

effects.log: A strange hill, strange voles, a strange owl. You are hungry all season. When you come back the brindle is still there, older, still with her nose on the dyke. (-3 health)

events.text: Dawn, and they have you. You hear the yellow dog's bell-voice from the stubble behind you, and then nothing, which is worse: the brindle running silent. The reed beds. You go in, and the dogs go in after you, and the master stands on the dyke with his bow, waiting for you to come out. It is going to be a long day. It is going to be three.

choices.text: Stay deep in the reeds and wait them out

ok.log: Three days in the reeds, in the mud, in the cold, drinking from the ditch and eating nothing. On the third night the master goes home. On the fourth morning, so do the dogs. You are still there.

fail.log: The brindle finds you on the second night and you run, out the far side, straight past the bow. The arrow takes a tuft of fur and nothing else. You do not stop till the ridge. (-8 health)

choices.text: Break out along the dyke at a run

ok.log: Out of the reeds, onto the dyke, flat out along the top of it with the dogs on the slope below, slower in the mud. A fox on a dyke is a thrown stone. You are over the stream before the master has his arrow on the string.

fail.log: The yellow dog is waiting on the dyke. Its teeth close on your tail and you leave it a mouthful. You get away. Your tail will never be quite so fine again. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go into the stream and let it take your scent away

effects.log: Cold enough to stop your heart. You let the current carry you down past the mill, and come out a long way off, half-dead and scentless. Behind you the dogs bark at the water. (-5 health)

events.text: At last, a grey morning. Mud to your belly, ribs showing, one ear torn. The dogs have gone home, but the brindle stops at the gate of the hunting household and looks back across the white fields toward where you are lying, for a long time. Then the gate closes. You are free, and you have been smelled twice, and you know that this is the one rule you can never keep again.

choices.text: Leave the east ridge for good

effects.log: You take a new earth on the west hill, past the old graves, and never cross the east dyke again in daylight. It is the first time you have run away from something and been proud of it.

choices.text: Go and look at the brindle from the ridge, once

effects.log: From the ridge you watch her lying in the yard with her nose on her paws. She lifts her head and looks at the ridge, straight at you, though there is no wind. Then she puts it down again. Something has been agreed, though you could not say what.

choices.text: Steal the master's hen on your way past, out of spite

ok.log: A hen from the hunter's own yard, under the noses of two exhausted dogs. The whole village laughs about it for a year. The hunter does not laugh. Ever.

fail.log: The yellow dog was not as tired as it looked. You get away, again, with nothing, again, and now the hunter has a reason. (-6 health)

events.text: Long years later a dog comes up the west hill alone, nose down, very old: brindle, with a torn ear. She cannot be the same dog. Dogs do not live twenty years. But she stops at the foot of your mound and lies down, and when you put your head out of the earth she looks at you with milky eyes and her tail moves once in the grass.

choices.text: Go out and lie down near her

effects.log: A pup of a pup of that brindle, perhaps, who learned your scent from the one before. She stays till dusk. Then she gets up stiffly and goes home. Twice is a hunt, the old rule says. Sometimes twice is something else.

choices.text: Stay in the earth until she goes

effects.log: You keep the rule. She lies there all afternoon, then goes. The next spring there is no brindle in the hunter's yard, and the new pup there is yellow, and loud, and knows nothing about you.

choices.text: Lead her home by the long way, in the dark

effects.log: She is half-blind and the night comes on. You go ahead of her along the dyke, close enough to smell, and she follows your smell all the way to her own gate. It is the strangest hunt either of you ever ran.

events.text: There is an old fox on the high ridge above the graves, older than anything on the hill: four tails, grey at the tips, and eyes like two lamps behind paper. You have only ever seen it at a distance. Tonight, at dusk, you see it go down the ridge path, stop behind the shrine pine, and turn over three times in the dead leaves. What gets up is an old woman in a white jacket, wearing something on her head that is not a hat.
events.arc: The Old Woman in the Hat

choices.text: Follow her down to the village

effects.log: She walks like an old woman, slow and bent, and stops to rest like one. Only her shadow walks like a fox. You follow at a distance in the long grass, holding your breath.

choices.text: Go and look at the place where she turned over

effects.log: Dead leaves, pressed flat in a circle, and a smell of fox and of something else, cold and very old, like the inside of a mound. You lie down in the circle. Nothing happens. Not yet.

choices.text: Keep well away from anything with four tails

effects.log: You go the other way, toward the paddies and the voles, where nothing is older than you are. It is wise. It is also, you will find, impossible to keep up for very long.

events.text: In the village they are all courtesy. An old woman alone on the road at dusk! The headman's household brings her in, seats her on the warm floor, sets a low table before her with rice and soup and pickled radish, and the headman's mother, who is old herself, sits with her and talks about knees. Nobody looks at the hat. Through the gap in the fence, you can see that nobody can.
events.arc: The Old Woman in the Hat

choices.text: Watch the old fox eat

effects.log: She eats like an old woman, slowly, thanking them for every dish. She asks after the headman's son, who is studying, and his grandson, who is sickly. She asks a great deal about the grandson.

choices.text: Watch the people instead

effects.log: They are kind. That is the whole trick. They are kind to an old woman because she is old and alone, and the kindness is real, and it is the door she walked in by. You do not like how much you understand it.

choices.text: Bark once at the gate, to see what happens

effects.log: The household dogs go mad. The old woman does not even turn her head. The headman curses the foxes on the hill and throws a stone into the dark, and the old woman thanks him for it, very softly.

events.text: A salt peddler comes up the village road in the last light, with his A-frame and his straw bags, and stops at the headman's gate for water. He drinks. He looks in through the gate at the old woman on the warm floor. He does not stop looking. Slowly, as if he had all the time in the world, he slips the A-frame off his back and props it on its forked stick, and then takes the stick away again, and holds it.
events.arc: The Old Woman in the Hat

choices.text: Bark a warning from the dark

effects.log: One sharp fox bark from the paddy. The old woman is up and through the back of the house before the peddler is through the gate. The village finds a hat that is not a hat on the floor, and screams for a week. On the ridge, four tails turn once toward you in the moonlight.

choices.text: Lie still and watch what a salt peddler does

effects.log: He does not hurry. He walks into the yard, up onto the porch, and says to the old woman, very politely: "Grandmother, your hat is on crooked." Everything that happens after that happens very fast.

choices.text: Run. This is not your fight

effects.log: You are over the dyke before the first shout. From the hill you hear the village wake: dogs, gongs, a crash, a long howl going up the ridge. In the morning, the ridge is quiet, and you do not know whose quiet it is.

events.text: In daylight you find the peddler on the hill road, resting, his A-frame propped on the forked stick, eating a rice ball. He has seen you. He goes on eating. When he is done he wipes his fingers, picks up the stick, and points it at the long grass where you are lying, not hard, the way one points at weather.
events.arc: The Old Woman in the Hat

choices.text: Stay where you are and look back at him

ok.log: "Not you," he says, to the grass. "Not yet. You have not done anything yet." He puts the stick back under the frame and walks on. You lie there till dark, and are not sure whether you have been forgiven or warned.

fail.log: He throws the rice-ball leaf at you, and the stick after it. The stick does not miss. Nothing that peddler throws ever misses. You limp for a month. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go, the long way round, and do not come back

effects.log: You never cross a salt peddler. It was the rule. Now you know why the rule had no exceptions.

choices.text: Creep close enough to smell the salt

effects.log: Salt and smoke and summer fire from the pans by the sea. The smell goes into your nose like a needle, and for a moment your own shape feels loose on you, like a coat. You run. You understand fire, now. (-3 health)

events.text: The old fox of the ridge has three tails now. One is gone, a stump, burned black. It sits on a rock above the graves at moonrise and looks down at you on your mound. "The salt peddler," it says, in the voice old foxes use with young ones, which is the voice of a grandmother who bites, "is the earth's way of telling a fox that it is a fox. Remember it. I did not."
events.arc: The Old Woman in the Hat

choices.text: Ask why it went down to the village at all

effects.log: "Hunger," it says. "And the warm floor. And the grandson." It does not explain the grandson. You decide never to ask about the grandson again.

choices.text: Tell it you barked that night

effects.log: "I know," it says. "I heard. Foxes pay their debts, small one, one way or the other." It does not sound grateful. It sounds like someone writing something down.

choices.text: Say nothing, and go down off the ridge

effects.log: You leave the old fox on its rock. Whatever it has to teach, you would rather learn it from the moon. The moon does not ask about grandsons.

events.text: A loop of twisted horsehair on the dyke, where the grass was flattened in just the way you like. It closes on your foreleg and holds. You pull, and it bites. You pull harder, and it bites harder. In the grey light a boy of the village, {npc}, comes along the dyke to look at the snares, and finds you, and stops.

choices.text: Go still and look {npc} in the eye

effects.log: You stop pulling and look at {npc}. {He} looks back. Nobody has ever looked at {him} like that, as if {he} were the one being decided about. {He} crouches down, slowly, a few steps off.

choices.text: Snap and snarl at {npc}

effects.log: You show every tooth you have and scream the way foxes scream. {npc} falls back on the dyke, white-faced, and then, to your surprise, laughs. "You are very small," {he} says, "to be so loud."

choices.text: Chew at the snare while {npc} watches

effects.log: You chew at the horsehair with {npc} watching, and {he} does not run for the grown-ups. {He} watches you hurt yourself for a while and then says, "Stop. Stop it. I will do it." (-6 health)

events.text: {npc} has a knife and a bad feeling about it. "My uncle pays for pelts," {he} says, to the fox and to {him}self. "Red ones. A whole coin." The knife comes down and cuts the horsehair, not you. {npc} sits back on {his} heels. "I want to see you again," {he} says. "That is the price. Come back to the dyke. Just to be seen."

choices.text: Come back to the dyke at dusk, now and then, to be seen

effects.log: You come at dusk and sit at the far end of the dyke, and {npc} sits at the near end, and neither of you moves. It goes on for years. {He} never tells {his} uncle. You never take a hen from {his} yard.

choices.text: Run, and never go near that dyke again

effects.log: You run on three legs and do not look back. {npc} waits at the dyke at dusk all that autumn. You know, because you watch {him} wait from the ridge, and are ashamed, and do not go down.

choices.text: Limp away, then turn and bow your head once

effects.log: A fox bowing on a dyke at dawn. {npc} will tell that story all {his} life, and nobody will ever believe {him}, and {he} will not mind.

events.text: Years later, a grown farmer on the dyke at dusk with a hoe over one shoulder: {npc}. {He} sits down at the near end, where {he} always sat. There is no snare anywhere on this dyke, nor on any dyke {he} farms, and there has not been for years. "They say there is a fox on the hill road now," {he} says, to the far end of the dyke, "that leads lost carters home. I said I knew it."

choices.text: Sit at the far end, the way you used to

effects.log: You sit till dark. {npc} talks about the harvest, the rain, a neighbour's quarrel, and you listen. When {he} goes {he} leaves half a rice ball on the dyke. It is the best thing you have eaten in ten years.

choices.text: Come close enough to be touched, once

ok.log: You walk the length of the dyke and stop an arm's length away. {npc} holds out a hand and does not move it. You smell it: earth, millet, an old cut from a sickle. Then you go. Some debts are paid by being seen.

fail.log: Halfway along the dyke your nerve goes, and you sit down, and so does {npc}. That is close enough. It was always close enough.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge. {He} is old enough now to stop believing

effects.log: You watch {npc} wait, the way you watched {him} as a child. {He} goes home before dark, and does not look disappointed. Some people do not need to be answered to keep believing.

events.text: Foxes do not dig. The vixen who raised you never dug; the old foxes never dig. They wait. And here, in an oak bank on the north slope, is the best earth you have ever smelled: deep, dry, many-roomed, lined with old bedding, and empty. An old badger dug it over forty winters, and has gone down to the stream to drink.

choices.text: Do what foxes do: foul the entrance and move in

effects.log: You leave your mark at every entrance and take the deepest room. It is a shameful trick and a very old one, and it works: badgers are clean, and cannot bear a fouled house. You sleep warm. You do not sleep well.

choices.text: Take the far room quietly, and hope it does not notice

effects.log: There are so many rooms. Surely one fox in a far room, quiet, clean, will be nothing to a badger. You curl up. You are, it turns out, wrong about badgers.

choices.text: Leave it. It is somebody's house

effects.log: You spend the first snow in a hollow under a rock, cold all through, and listen to the badger come home to its warm earth and snore. (-3 health)

events.text: The badger comes back. It is the size of a small dog and the shape of a closed door, and it stands in the entrance with its striped face full of fury, smelling fox in every room of its house. It does not leave. It comes in.

choices.text: Stand your ground in the tunnel

ok.log: A long, close, dirty fight in the dark. The badger backs out at last, muttering, and goes to dig a new house on the next bank. You have won a house. You do not feel like someone who has won.

fail.log: Badgers do not let go. You come out of the far entrance a long time later with a bitten foreleg and nothing else, and the badger goes back to bed. (-12 health)

choices.text: Back out the far entrance, and let it have its house

effects.log: There is always a far entrance in a badger sett. That is the first thing you learn about them. The second is that they never forget a fox.

choices.text: Lie very still in the far room and see what it does

effects.log: It sniffs every room. It stops at yours. It looks at you for a long time with small, cross, short-sighted eyes, grunts, and goes to bed in the deepest room. Apparently, if you do not foul the house, a badger has opinions, but no objections.

events.text: Deep winter in the sett. The badger sleeps most of the season and snores like a cart on a bad road. On warm days it wakes, eats worms, scolds you, and digs a new room nobody needs, for the sake of digging. You have never been so warm, or so lectured.

choices.text: Watch it dig

effects.log: It digs the way the salt peddler walks: not in a hurry, never lost. Forty winters of one bank. You think of your own life, all foxes' lives, borrowed houses and other people's work. It is the first time you have wanted to make something.

choices.text: Bring it a share of everything you catch

effects.log: A vole, a frog, half a hen. It takes them all without thanks, as rent. In spring, when you go, it comes to the entrance and grunts at you once. You decide it was goodbye.

choices.text: Sleep through the winter like it does

effects.log: You sleep, it sleeps, the snow sleeps on top of the bank. In spring you are rested in a way you did not know a fox could be. Badgers know things.

events.text: An autumn night on the red marsh below the graves, and your tail is doing something it has never done: at the tip of it, when you flick it, a small cold light comes off and floats away over the reeds, orange as a persimmon. Foxfire. And over the black water on the far side, other lights are moving, pale blue, low and wandering, which are not yours.

choices.text: Flick your tail again, and again, and watch the lights go

effects.log: Five lights, six, a dozen, hanging over the reeds like a lantern festival nobody came to. A man on the far dyke stops, stares, and starts walking toward them, off the path. You stop at once.

choices.text: Go round the marsh to see whose the blue lights are

ok.log: Behind a hummock of reeds, a squat, hairy, one-legged shape is juggling blue fire with enormous delight and humming a song badly. A dokkaebi. It has not noticed you. Nobody notices you, when a dokkaebi is enjoying itself.

fail.log: You go into the marsh after the blue lights and the marsh goes into you, up to your chin. By the time you crawl out they are gone, and you are a mud fox. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lie still and learn the difference between the two fires

effects.log: Yours is warm-coloured and cold to the touch; it goes where you send it. The blue ones are cold-coloured and warm, and go wherever they like. Somebody is having more fun than you are.

events.text: A dokkaebi is sitting on your favourite hummock, waiting for you, with a club across its knees and a face like a wrinkled radish. "You," it says. "Fox. You have been leading MY travellers off MY path with YOUR lights. A carter full of makgeolli, last month. I had plans for that carter. It is very rude." It stands up on its one leg. "We will wrestle for the marsh."

choices.text: Wrestle it

ok.log: Dokkaebi always fall to the left. Somebody told you that once, or you dreamed it. You throw it to the left. It lies on its back in the reeds, laughing so hard it cannot get up. "Again!" it says. "Tomorrow! Again!"

fail.log: It throws you into the marsh, picks you out, throws you in again, and is very pleased with itself. "Two falls to nothing," it says. "Rude AND weak." It is starting to like you. You can tell. (-8 health)

choices.text: Apologise, with a bow, very low

effects.log: It looks at you suspiciously for a long time. "Nobody apologises to a dokkaebi," it says. "Is this a trick?" It is a little bit a trick. It is also a little bit an apology. The dokkaebi, satisfied, sits back down.

choices.text: Lead it astray with your own lights

ok.log: You send a dozen foxfires off across the marsh and the dokkaebi, which cannot help itself, goes hopping after them. You hear it laughing out in the dark for an hour. When it comes back it is in the best mood of its life.

fail.log: It knows foxfire when it sees it. It brings your lights back to you in its fist, one by one, and drops them on your head. They do not burn. The humiliation does. (-5 health)

events.text: The dokkaebi comes back at the next new moon with a wooden bowl of buckwheat jelly, wobbling and grey, the food dokkaebi love more than anything. "Peace," it says. "Even nights are mine. Odd nights are yours. Carters full of makgeolli we share." It holds out the bowl. It is clearly very hard for it to hold out the bowl.

choices.text: Accept the bowl and the bargain

effects.log: The jelly tastes of nothing much and the dokkaebi watches every mouthful as if it were watching a child eat its own heart. It keeps the bargain for a hundred years. Dokkaebi are terrible at most things, and very good at bargains.

choices.text: Give it the bowl back, and the whole marsh with it

effects.log: "All of it?" It is so shocked it nearly drops the jelly. "Why?" Because the marsh was its first, you say, in fox. It does not understand a word, and understands you perfectly, and eats the whole bowl itself, crying a little.

choices.text: Ask for the carters on odd nights too

effects.log: It argues for an hour, delighted. You settle on every third carter, and lame horses are always yours. You both feel you have won. That is how you know it was a good bargain.

events.text: Midnight on the hill of the old graves, where nobody has come to cut the grass for a hundred years. The mounds are low and soft as sleeping animals. Out of the oldest of them, when the air is still, comes a breath: not wind, not mist, but something cold and slow that you can taste, like water from a deep well. It goes into your mouth if you let it.

choices.text: Let it in

effects.log: It goes down cold and stays cold. The rice grain of light behind your teeth drinks it, and brightens, and something in your chest goes a little quieter than it was. (+2 Bead)

choices.text: Taste it, and spit it out

effects.log: It tastes of very old things: iron, cold earth, a name nobody says any more. You spit. The old graves do not mind. They have been refused before.

choices.text: Sit with your back to the mounds and watch the village lights instead

effects.log: The cold breath comes and goes behind you. In front, far below, somebody's lamp is still lit at midnight: a student, perhaps, or a sick child. You watch it till it goes out, and go home warm.

events.text: At noon a geomancer comes up the hill with a round wooden compass, its face ringed with tiny characters, and a young apprentice carrying an umbrella over it. He walks the slope, stops, turns the compass, mutters, walks. "Here the dragon of the hill lies down," he tells the apprentice, poking the earth with a stick. "Here it turns its head. Here it breathes." He is pointing straight at the oldest mound.

choices.text: Follow them all afternoon, downwind

effects.log: By dusk you know where the earth's qi runs on this hill, and it is not quite where the geomancer said. He is off by a few paces at the turning of the head. You decide not to tell him. You could not, anyway.

choices.text: Lie on the mound he pointed at, to feel what he means

effects.log: Under the grass, under the soil, the hill breathes: slowly, a breath a season. Your own breath slows to match it. When you open your eyes the geomancer is gone and it is dark.

choices.text: Trip the apprentice with the umbrella, for fun

effects.log: The apprentice goes down, the umbrella goes up, the compass spins. "A fox!" "A fox on a grave at noon," says the geomancer, very thoughtfully, "is either very good luck or very bad." He writes it down. You are in a book now.

events.text: A burial on the lower slope: a poor family, no geomancer, a plain coffin, and a site chosen because it was free. It is wet. You know it is wet; the water runs under that spot every spring, cold and wrong, and the dead there will lie in it. The stake for the grave is already in. A few paces up the slope the earth is dry and breathes.

choices.text: Move the stake in the night, up the slope

ok.log: You dig the stake out with your teeth and paws and drag it six paces up. In the morning the family digs where it stands, and finds the ground dry, and is grateful to nobody in particular. The hill breathes over that grave for a hundred years.

fail.log: The eldest son is sitting up with the coffin and sees a fox dragging the grave stake. He chases you with a lamp, then stands for a long time where you dropped it, and digs there. Dry ground. He never tells anyone why.

choices.text: Leave it. The dead are not your business

effects.log: They bury their father in the wet place. In spring the water runs under it, as it always has. The family is unlucky for three generations and never knows why. You know why.

choices.text: Go and sit by the wet place, so they see a fox there and wonder

effects.log: A fox sitting on the chosen spot, staring at them. The mother says it is an omen and makes them dig higher up. You have never been called an omen before. You find you like it.

events.text: Too many nights on the old graves. The cold has gone in deep. You notice it first in small ways: a hare goes past and you feel nothing, not hunger, not fun, nothing; the village lights look far away and flat, like lights painted on a screen. The bead behind your teeth is brighter than it has ever been, and colder.

choices.text: Stop. Go down to the paddies and the warm things

effects.log: You spend a season among frogs and voles and farm dogs and the smell of cooking. The warmth comes back slowly, the way feeling comes back to a frozen paw: it hurts. You are glad it hurts.

choices.text: Keep going. Cold is power

effects.log: You go on breathing the cold of the old dead every night of the season. The bead takes it all, and glows like ice under the moon. You do not notice, this time, what goes out of you. That is what the cold does. (+2 Bead)

choices.text: Ask the geomancer's hill what it wants

effects.log: You lie on the breathing mound and ask, in the only way a fox can ask. The hill does not answer. But the cold stops coming up for you, that night, as if something had decided you had taken enough.

events.text: Your first full moon as a grown fox, alone on the mound. You sit the way she sat, upright, with your face turned up, and breathe in slowly through your mouth. Nothing happens. The moon goes over. A dog barks in the village. Nothing happens. Near dawn, on the very last breath, something cold and small settles on your tongue like a snowflake that does not melt.

choices.text: Close your mouth on it and keep it

effects.log: You go home with your mouth shut tight, afraid to yawn. In the earth you open it a crack, carefully. A rice grain of pale light, behind your teeth. Dim as a coal under ash. Yours. (+3 Bead)

choices.text: Bow to the moon, the way you saw her do

effects.log: You put your forehead down on the frosty grass, three times, and the cold thing in your mouth stays. You do not know who taught foxes to bow. You suspect it was the moon. (+3 Bead)

choices.text: Try to swallow it and see what happens

effects.log: It will not go down. It sits behind your teeth and will not go down, however you swallow, and makes you cough until the dog in the village starts barking again. It belongs in the mouth. Of course it does. (-4 health, +2 Bead)

events.text: Every full moon for a year, on the mound, breathing. The rice grain is still a rice grain, but it is a warmer colour now, and in the dark of the earth you can see your own paws by it. It is the only thing in the world you have ever owned. You catch yourself, in the daytime, checking with your tongue that it is still there.

choices.text: Keep the full moons, every one, even in rain

effects.log: Even in rain, even with the dogs out, even the night the snow came sideways. The moon behind the cloud still counts, you find, if you sit as if it did not. (+3 Bead)

choices.text: Bow on the half moons too, to hurry it

effects.log: The half moons give half as much and take twice as long to sit through. The bead does not hurry. It grows the way trees grow: whether you watch it or not. (+2 Bead)

choices.text: Show it to the dokkaebi, or the badger, or anyone

effects.log: You open your mouth to show someone and remember the third rule just in time, and close it, and pretend to yawn. Nobody else will ever see it if you can help it. (+2 Bead)

events.text: The harvest moon, red and enormous, coming up over the paddies like a lantern somebody is carrying up the hill. You sit on the mound and breathe, and the bead in your mouth answers. You feel it: a small warmth, then a glow you can see on the grass in front of you, faint, the colour of the inside of a shell. The village dogs, all of them at once, stop barking.

choices.text: Hold the glow as long as you can

effects.log: Until moonset. The glow on the grass goes, but the bead stays bright behind your teeth, a little brighter than a rice grain now. The moon has noticed you. You are sure of it. (+4 Bead)

choices.text: Close your mouth on it, quickly, before anyone sees

effects.log: Dark again on the mound. Below, the dogs start up, one by one, as if they had all forgotten what they were barking about and remembered. A light on a grave mound on the harvest moon: by morning the whole village will have a story. (+4 Bead)

choices.text: Bow, and give thanks to whoever is listening

effects.log: You bow to the moon, and to the mound, and to the old dead under it, who have kept you warm all these years and asked nothing. The bead glows under your forehead in the frost. Heaven counts this kind. (+4 Bead)

events.text: On the jar platform of the last farmhouse by the dyke there is a tall water jar that is warm. In the first frost. Every other jar has ice on its lid, and this one breathes out a faint warmth that you can feel from the wall, like a sleeping animal. Your tail, which is always cold, aches toward it.

choices.text: Lie against the jar for a night

effects.log: Warm as a hearth, warm right through. You sleep against it as you have not slept since the pile in the first earth. Near dawn, something inside the jar moves, and the warmth goes cold, and you run.

choices.text: Look into the water

ok.log: Under the water, curled on the bottom of the jar, something blue-green and very small, with whiskers. It opens one eye and looks at you. It is not afraid. It is curious, the way you were curious in the first earth.

fail.log: You put your forepaws on the rim and lean, and the lid slides, and the farmhouse dog arrives before the lid hits the stones. You leave without seeing anything. (-4 health)

choices.text: Leave it. Warm things in jars are somebody's

effects.log: You go home to your cold earth and lie with your tail over your nose. Whatever is in the jar, the old woman of the house clearly knows it is there: she has put a little dish of rice beside it.

events.text: It is a dragonet, no longer than your foreleg, blue-green, with soft whiskers and the stubs of horns. It lives in the farmhouse water jar and the old woman feeds it rice and talks to it about the weather. It is warm the way the sun is warm: from the inside. A fox who lay against that warmth all winter, the old foxes say, might grow a tail a century early.

choices.text: Lie against the jar every night, and take the warmth

effects.log: All winter. You feel your tail fill out, warmer, heavier. The dragonet in the jar grows quieter, slower, colder each night. It knows what is happening. It looks at you through the water, every night, and remembers.

choices.text: Guard the jar from the weasel that has been watching it

ok.log: The weasel comes on the coldest night, for the warm thing in the jar. You meet it on the jar platform. It goes. The dragonet watches the whole fight with its chin on the rim, and when you limp away, it blows one bubble after you.

fail.log: The weasel bites you, you bite the weasel, the jars rattle, the old woman comes out with a lamp. The weasel runs. So do you. The dragonet saw which of you stayed longest. (-6 health)

choices.text: Leave it alone, and leave it warm

effects.log: You go back to the cold earth. Your tail stays thin and cold all winter, and grows its own way, slowly, like everything honest.

events.text: The water jar is empty. The old woman sits beside it on the jar platform with her hands in her lap, looking at the paddies. The dragonet has gone down into the paddy water, she tells the dog, which is the only one listening: too big for a jar now. You can see where it went: a long ripple in the flooded field, and the frogs all silent.

choices.text: Follow the ripple along the dyke

ok.log: At the end of the paddy the ripple stops, and a blue-green head the size of a dog's comes up out of the water and looks at you. It knows you. Whatever you did, it knows. Then it sinks, and the frogs start up again.

fail.log: The ripple goes under the dyke and does not come out. Dragons, it turns out, can be very hard to follow when they want to be.

choices.text: Sit with the old woman, at a distance

effects.log: She sees you, a fox on her wall, and does not shoo you. "You too," she says. "You miss it too." You do not, exactly. But you sit there until her lamp is lit, because she seems to need somebody to.

choices.text: Go home. A dragon is no business of a fox's

effects.log: You go home along the far side of the dyke, away from the water. The old foxes say dragons and foxes have hated each other since the beginning. You do not want to find out why. Not yet.

events.text: A summer storm comes down on the paddies with a sound like a hundred drums, and in the middle of it, just for a moment, you see a long blue-green shape in the rain over the flooded fields, no longer small, turning its head. Toward the hill. Toward you. The rain on your mound stops, all at once, as if somebody had put a hand over it.

choices.text: Bow to it, in the dry on your mound

effects.log: A fox bowing in a dry circle in the middle of a storm. The shape in the rain looks at you for a long moment. Then the rain comes back, softly, and you are only a fox again, getting wet.

choices.text: Stare back at it

effects.log: You look at it, and it looks at you, across the storm. Neither of you looks away. It is the first time you understand why foxes and dragons do not like each other: neither of you knows how to lose a stare.

choices.text: Go down into the earth and stay there

effects.log: You go down, and the storm goes on over the hill. In the morning there is a single blue-green scale on the grass of your mound, the size of a coin. You hide it in the deepest room. Whatever it means, it is yours now.

events.text: Rain from a clear sky. The sun is out, there is not a cloud anywhere, and big bright drops are falling on the paddies, each one lit up gold. You and your mother sit under a hedge and watch it. "A tiger is taking a bride somewhere," she says. "The sky laughs and cries at once. People call this rain after us, because they think only a fox could play such a trick."

choices.text: Ask her if it is a fox trick

effects.log: "Not this time," she says. "This one is the tigers'. But they will blame us. They always blame us. Remember that, when you have tricks of your own."

choices.text: Run out into it

effects.log: You run along the dyke with your mouth open, catching sun-rain. Every drop tastes faintly of something you cannot name, something wild and far off and happy.

choices.text: Look for the tigers

effects.log: There is nothing on the hills but light. Your mother laughs at you, a fox's laugh, which is mostly breath. "You will not see them," she says. "Nobody sees them."

events.text: Another sunshower, years on, and you are watching for it this time. Through the shining rain and the mist coming up off the warm stones, on the far ridge, a line of great striped shapes walks slowly along the skyline, one behind another: old ones in front, two side by side, young ones tumbling at the back. No sound reaches you at all. Nothing on the whole mountain moves.

choices.text: Lie flat under the hedge and watch

effects.log: You watch until the rain stops and the ridge is only a ridge. Your fur is standing on end from nose to tail. You have just seen something you were never meant to see, and lived. That is a fox's whole art.

choices.text: Keep pace along your own ridge

ok.log: You run along your ridge as they walk along theirs, a red spark keeping pace with a slow river of stripes. At the end of the rain they turn their heads, all of them, and look across the valley at you. Then the sun is only sun.

fail.log: You slip on the wet rock and roll down half the hill. When you look up, the rain has stopped and the far ridge is bare. (-4 health)

choices.text: Go down into your earth. Tigers are not for looking at

effects.log: You spend the sunshower underground. Wise. Afterwards, you think about it for a year, which is not wise, but is very fox.

events.text: The first sunshower of a summer, and when it stops you find it on the far bank of the stream that divides your hill from the tigers' mountain: a young striped tiger lying on a wet rock in the sun, about your age in tiger years, which is to say enormous. It has been watching you for a while. It does not get up. It only looks, the way the brindle looked, as if something were being agreed.

choices.text: Sit down on your bank, and look back

effects.log: A fox and a tiger on two sides of a stream, looking. After a long time it yawns, which shows every tooth it has, and goes back up its mountain. You decide that was a greeting. You will find out, much later, that it was.

choices.text: Leave a frog on a stone in the stream, as a courtesy

effects.log: It looks at the frog as if nobody had ever given it anything so small in its life. Then it eats it, gravely, and leaves. The next sunshower there is a whole pheasant on the stone.

choices.text: Go. Fast

effects.log: You are three hills away before the tiger has finished its yawn. It is not a trick. It is not cowardice either. It is a fox knowing exactly how big it is.

events.text: The village school is one room on a raised floor, and under the floor, between the stone footings, it is cool and dusty and smells of straw sandals. Above you, all summer, children chant: "Heaven, dark. Earth, yellow." Over and over, a little louder when the teacher coughs. You lie under the boards with your chin on your paws and listen.

choices.text: Chant along, silently, in your head

effects.log: Heaven, dark. Earth, yellow. The universe, vast and wild. By the end of summer you know the first hundred sounds, and what some of them mean, and you lie awake at night saying them to the pine roots.

choices.text: Watch the children's feet go in and out

effects.log: Small feet, dusty feet, one with a bandaged toe, one who is always late and always running. You learn them all by their walk before you learn a word. People are their feet, to a fox.

choices.text: Steal a sandal, for fun

effects.log: You take one straw sandal to the edge of the paddy and leave it there. The uproar is wonderful. The teacher says it is a fox, and the children say it is a ghost, and they are both nearly right.

events.text: The teacher knows you are under the floor. You are sure of it, because every evening, after the children have gone, an old man in a worn grey robe comes out onto the step, sits for a while looking at the paddies, and leaves behind him, as if by accident, a rice ball wrapped in a leaf.

choices.text: Take the rice ball, and leave the leaf folded neatly

effects.log: Every evening, a rice ball; every morning, a folded leaf. Neither of you mentions it. It goes on for years. It is the first conversation you ever have with a human, and there is not a single word in it.

choices.text: Leave the rice ball, and listen to him instead

effects.log: He talks to the paddies when he thinks nobody is listening: about a student who will pass and one who will not, about his knees, about an old story of a fox and a bead and a boy who looked at the sky. You lie very still for that one.

choices.text: Show yourself at the end of the step

ok.log: He looks at you a long time. "Heaven, dark," he says. "Earth, yellow." You tilt your head. He laughs, a dry old laugh. "Do not tell the children," he says, "that a fox is ahead of half of them."

fail.log: He sees you and throws his shoe, out of habit. Then he looks sorry. The next evening there are two rice balls. (-3 health)

events.text: A child finishes the Thousand Character Classic, the whole book, and there is a book-party: rice cakes for everyone, the teacher pretending to be stern, the child red with pride. Under the floor, you can say the whole thing too, every one of the thousand, though you have never held a brush. Above you the teacher says, to nobody, "There is one more student who finished. I will save a rice cake."

choices.text: Take the rice cake from the step, proudly

effects.log: A whole rice cake, for a whole book. You eat it on the mound under the moon, slowly. It is the first thing anyone ever gave you for something you did, not something you are.

choices.text: Scratch a character in the dust of the step

ok.log: One character, scratched with a claw: heaven. In the morning the teacher looks at it for a long time, then sweeps it away very carefully, so nobody else sees. He knows what he knows. So do you.

fail.log: What you scratch looks like a chicken walked through the dust. Which, the next morning, is what the teacher decides happened.

choices.text: Stay under the floor, and let the child have the day

effects.log: It is the child's day. You lie in the dust and listen to the party, and the teacher's rice cake goes stale on the step, and is found by ants. It was still a good day.

events.text: The village holds a rite for the new year: drums, a table piled with rice cakes and a pig's head and paper flowers, and a shaman in a red robe dancing with a painted fan and a cluster of brass bells. You watch from the dark edge of the firelight with the other night creatures: the cat, an owl, something under the bridge. The shaman stops dancing. The bells go quiet. She turns, and looks straight into the dark, at you.

choices.text: Hold her eyes

effects.log: "You," she says to the dark, in an ordinary voice. "Not tonight." The villagers look at each other. She shakes the bells and dances on. You are halfway home before you realise she was not threatening you. She was telling you to go.

choices.text: Back away into the grass

effects.log: You go, slowly, and the bells start again behind you. From the hill you watch the rite go on all night. Something was decided about you in that look. You would like very much to know what.

choices.text: Steal a rice cake from the table while everyone stares at the dark

ok.log: Everyone is looking where the shaman looked, and you are not there any more: you are at the table, then gone, with a rice cake. The shaman laughs out loud, the only one who saw. It becomes the village's favourite story about her.

fail.log: The shaman's drummer sees you and throws a drumstick. It is a very good throw. (-5 health)

events.text: The shaman comes up the hill road alone at dusk, an old woman with her bells tied in a cloth at her belt, and sits on a stone near your mound. "I know you are there," she says. "Foxes and shamans are cousins. We both stand between. You have not done anything yet. That is why I said not tonight." She takes a rice cake out of her sleeve and puts it on the stone.

choices.text: Come out and take it from beside her

effects.log: You come out of the grass and take the cake from the stone a hand's width from her knee. She does not look at you. She talks about the weather, and her knees, and the year, the way old people do. Old people talk to foxes. You are starting to understand why.

choices.text: Stay hidden and listen

effects.log: "When you have a face," she says to the grass, "and you will, come and see me first, before anyone else. A face without a name is a mask. A face with a name is a debt. Choose the debt." She leaves. You think about it for years.

choices.text: Lead her home with foxfire, since it is getting dark

effects.log: A small orange light floats ahead of her all the way down the hill road to her gate. She does not hurry and does not look back. At the gate she bows to it, very correctly, and goes in.

events.text: The shaman is dying. You know before the village does: the bells at her belt have stopped, and her gate has been shut two days. On the third night you go down to the gate. Inside, a lamp. Her voice, thin: "Is that you? Come in, cousin. Nobody else will come in at night."

choices.text: Go in and lie by the door

effects.log: You lie by the door all night, and she talks, and sometimes sleeps, and sometimes calls you by other names. Near dawn she says, "Choose the debt," again, and nothing else. In the morning the village finds her at peace, and a fox print in the dust by the door.

choices.text: Sit at the gate, and keep the dogs away

effects.log: Three dogs come in the night, the way dogs come to a house where someone is dying. You send them off, every one. At dawn the bells in their cloth on the step ring once by themselves. Then nothing.

choices.text: Go back up the hill. You cannot bear it

effects.log: You go back to the mound and sit with your back to the village all night. In the morning they ring the bell for her. You count the strokes. You will be sorry about this for a hundred years.

events.text: Dusk among the old graves, and a small voice crying: a child of the village, {npc}, sent up for kindling, has come too far and lost the path among the mounds, which all look the same in the half dark. {He} is sitting on the wettest one, the one over the cold spring, and it is getting colder.

choices.text: Walk ahead with a light on your tail

effects.log: One small orange light, at the height of a child's knee, going slowly ahead between the mounds. {npc} stops crying and follows it. You go all the way to the village gate, and stop, and let the light go out.

choices.text: Show yourself, and walk ahead slowly, looking back

ok.log: A fox, ten paces off, walking and stopping and looking back. {npc} gets up and follows, because nothing in the world is more interesting than a fox that waits for you. At the village gate you stop. {He} runs in, shouting.

fail.log: {npc} sees a fox in the dusk and screams, and screams, until the whole village comes up the hill with torches and finds {him}. That works too. You watch from the pines.

choices.text: Bark until the village hears

effects.log: Fox barks carry. Somebody in the village says "fox in the graveyard", and somebody else says "where is {npc}?", and then there are torches on the hill. You go before they arrive.

choices.text: It is not your business. Let the people find {npc}

effects.log: They find {npc} at midnight, cold and hoarse, on the wet mound. {He} lives. You tell yourself that was always going to happen.

events.text: In the village nobody believes {npc}. "A fox led me home," {he} tells everyone, "and waited at every turn." Foxes lead people astray, the grown-ups say; everybody knows that. A fox in the graveyard is the worst thing in the world. {npc} is made to wear a charm and keep away from the hill. {He} does not keep away from the hill.

choices.text: Let {npc} find you on the hill, at a distance

effects.log: A child at the edge of the graves, a fox at the edge of the pines. {npc} waves. You do not know how to wave. You sit down, which seems to be the right answer.

choices.text: Keep away, so {npc} stops getting into trouble

effects.log: You stay out of sight all year. {npc} comes up the hill every week anyway, and leaves things on a stone: a persimmon, a pretty pebble, a rice cake with one bite out of it. You take them all.

choices.text: Lead a singing carter home past {npc}'s house, so someone else has seen

effects.log: Old Kim the carter, singing, led home by a light that stops at that very gate. Next day the carter tells the whole village. Now there are two people nobody believes. {npc} is delighted.

events.text: {npc} is grown now, with a farm at the bottom of the hill, and on summer nights {he} sits on the porch and tells the village children the story of the fox in the graveyard who walks ahead with a light. The children do not believe {him} either. But none of them, ever, is afraid of the hill road after dark.

choices.text: Walk past the porch one night, a little light on your tail

effects.log: One small orange light goes along the bottom of the hill, past the porch, and out. The children scream with delight. {npc} does not say anything at all. {He} just smiles, the way people smile when they have been right for a very long time.

choices.text: Leave a persimmon on {his} step

effects.log: In the morning {npc} finds a persimmon on the step, with tooth marks. {He} keeps the stone. Years later, there is a persimmon tree at that gate, and the village calls it the fox tree.

choices.text: Let it be a story. Stories outlive foxes

effects.log: You do not go down. The story goes on without you, and changes, and grows a better fox than you are. That is what stories do. You find you do not mind being improved.

events.text: The village has a new name for the hill road: the Fox's Road. Mothers tell their children that if they are lost after dark they should look for a small orange light at the height of their knee and follow it, and not run. Nobody knows where the custom came from. One old farmer at the bottom of the hill could tell them, and smiles.

choices.text: Keep the custom true

effects.log: For the rest of your years on the hill, no child is lost on the Fox's Road for long. Somewhere in heaven, you suspect, somebody is counting this kind of thing.

choices.text: Be proud of it, a little

effects.log: A road with your name in it. You walk the length of it at midnight with your tail up, very pleased with yourself, and are nearly caught by a dog. Pride, the vixen who raised you would have said, smiling.

events.text: Walking ahead of {npc} between the mounds, you have the strangest feeling: that you have done this before, on another hill, for another child, and that the child threw a stone at the light, a good hard stone, and was led home anyway. Somewhere a soul remembers being that child. It is not angry with you. It is, very faintly, embarrassed.

choices.text: Forgive the stone, whoever threw it

effects.log: You never held it against anyone. Children throw stones at lights. That is what lights are for, partly. {npc} does not throw anything. You find you are a little disappointed.

choices.text: Walk a little farther from {npc} this time, just in case

effects.log: Twelve paces instead of ten. {npc} follows the light all the same. Old lessons, from lives that were not even yours. Foxes keep everything.

events.text: At the village gate, {npc} turns round in the dark and bows to the light, very correctly, the way grown-ups bow, and says thank you. Nobody taught {him} that. And yet you have been bowed to like this before, at another gate, by another lost child who grew up and lived a whole life and died and is, somewhere, still bowing.

choices.text: Bow back, with your whole body

effects.log: A fox bowing at a village gate at night to a child bowing back. Nobody sees it but the guardian posts. They have seen stranger things, but not many.

choices.text: Let the light go out slowly, like a lamp being turned down

effects.log: It fades the way a good evening fades. {npc} watches it until it is gone, then goes in. Two lives, two bows. Heaven counts this kind of thing. You are sure of it now.

events.text: {npc} follows the light all the way down without once looking away from it, the way some children follow a story, and you feel a soul behind {him}, very old, that followed a light like this once among other graves and never forgot it. It is as if two children were following you, one inside the other.

choices.text: Make the light a little brighter, for both of them

effects.log: A small orange light at the height of a child's knee, brighter than you have ever made it. Both of them follow it home. Only one of them goes in at the gate.

choices.text: Stop at the gate and wait to see if the old soul says anything

effects.log: It does not speak. Souls do not, much. But {npc} looks back at the dark where you are, a long look, an old look, before going in.

events.text: The rice failed in the summer, and then the barley, and now it is winter and there is nothing. No voles in the stubble: the village children dug them all out and ate them. No hens: the village ate them. The pines on your hill have pale patches where the people have stripped the inner bark to boil in lye and eat. The smoke has gone out of half the chimneys.

choices.text: Hunt farther, over the ridges

ok.log: Two ridges over, in the valley with no village, there are still hares. You come back thin and alive. Most foxes on your hill do not come back.

fail.log: Two ridges, three, and nothing. You come home on legs that shake and lie in the earth for a week. (-10 health)

choices.text: Dig for kudzu roots on the south slope, like the people do

effects.log: The people dig them for the starch. You dig beside them, at night, in the holes they left. It is hardly food. It is enough to not die. You understand the people better than you ever wanted to. (-3 health)

choices.text: Lie still in the earth and spend as little as you can

effects.log: You sleep, and wake, and sleep. Your breathing gets slower and slower, like the hill's. The cold goes in. Something in you learns a stillness that is almost like the moon. (-6 health)

events.text: An old beggar, {npc}, has lain down by the hill road at the edge of the graves, too weak to go on to the next village. It is dusk. {He} is asleep, or nearly, and {his} breath is very slow, and very warm, in the cold air: a thread of warmth you can see, rising. You are so hungry. You do not know why that breath makes you hungry. You will know, one day.

choices.text: Lie down near {npc}, to keep the cold off

effects.log: All night, your back against {his} side. {He} wakes at dawn with a fox curled against {him} and does not scream: {he} is too tired. {He} puts a hand on your back. In the morning a cart comes by and takes {him} to the next village. (-3 health)

choices.text: Run to the village and bark at the nearest gate

effects.log: A household comes out to curse the fox and finds a beggar on the road. They have nothing. They share it anyway. You watch from the dark and are not sure which of you is more surprised.

choices.text: Walk past. You cannot feed anyone

effects.log: You go on along the road and do not look back. In the morning the beggar is gone: a cart, or the next village, or somewhere else. You never find out which. You make sure not to.

events.text: The old fox of the ridge finds you in your earth, thin as a stick. It is thin too, but not like you: its coat is full and its eyes are bright. "There is another way to eat in a famine," it says, "the old way. The oldest. I could teach you. You would never be hungry again." It does not say what the old way is. It does not need to. You can smell the village on it.

choices.text: Refuse, and go hungry

effects.log: "No," you say. The old fox looks at you a long time. "Then you will be a small fox all your life," it says, and goes. You lie in the dark and are hungry, and hungry, and you are still yourself in the morning. (-8 health)

choices.text: Ask it why it does not go hungry like everyone else

effects.log: "Because I am old," it says, "and the old way is how I got old." It waits. You do not follow. When it is gone you realise that was the lesson: not the way, but what it costs. It shows in its eyes.

choices.text: Follow it down to the village, on the night with no moon

effects.log: You go down with it in the dark, and come back alone before dawn, and are not hungry. You do not let yourself think about why. In the spring there is one more grave on the lower slope than there was. You never go near it. (A life is on you now.)

events.text: Spring, and the barley comes in at last, green over the paddies, and the smoke comes back into the chimneys one by one. The people who are left go out into the fields thin as ghosts and cut the first barley before it is ripe and eat it green. On the hill, the stripped pines are healing over. So is something in you, or not.

choices.text: Go down and walk the paddy dykes in the sun

effects.log: A child sees you on the dyke and does not throw a stone. Everyone is too tired to hate a fox this spring. You walk the whole length of the dykes in the sun, alive, and so are they.

choices.text: Visit the new graves on the lower slope

effects.log: A row of them, small and raw. You sit by them for a night. You did not kill the famine; you only lived through it. But you are a fox of the graves, and these are your neighbours now.

choices.text: Promise the moon you will never be that hungry again

effects.log: You do not know how you will keep it. The moon does not ask. It only listens, the way it always has.

events.text: A trader comes to the five-day market with a pole of pelts over his shoulder: marten, weasel, a badger, a dozen red fox. He calls the village boys round and tells them: a coin for a red fox pelt, good condition, no holes. Two for a white. "The governor's people pay well for white," he says. "A white fox is worth a whole autumn's work." You think of White-Paw, and its two white forepaws, as if it had stepped in snow.

choices.text: Go north along the stream to warn White-Paw
