effects.log: Three nights north you find it, grown, with a mate and a litter in a bank above a ford. You do not have words for what you want to say. You sit with it till dawn. It understands enough to move its earth.

choices.text: Watch which boys go home with snares

effects.log: Six boys, by nightfall, are twisting horsehair in their yards. You learn every one of their faces, and which dykes their families farm, and you will not forget them for a long time.

choices.text: Lead the trader off the road, into the marsh, on his way home

effects.log: Lights in the reeds, and a trader who has had too much of the market's makgeolli follows them off the dyke and into the marsh to his waist. He loses three pelts and his hat. The village decides it was the fox on the hill, and for once the village is right.

events.text: The first snow, and word comes along the stream the way word comes among foxes: in scent marks, in the way the crows gather. A white fox has been snared at the ford. Not dead yet. The boy who set the snare has gone home for his uncle's knife, and it is a long walk home, and it is getting dark.

choices.text: Run north to the ford

ok.log: You run all night along the stream and find White-Paw at the ford, half-frozen, one foreleg in the horsehair. You chew it through. White-Paw limps off into the reeds without a word, as foxes do. You sit in the snow and shake for an hour.

fail.log: You run all night and get there at dawn, and there is only the snare, cut, and the snow trampled by boots. On the next market day the trader has a white pelt on his pole, with two snow-white forepaws. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go to the boy's yard and take his uncle's knife

ok.log: A knife on a chopping block in a yard. You take it in your teeth and drop it in the well. By the time they find another knife it is morning, and the snare at the ford is empty, and chewed, and there are two sets of fox tracks in the snow.

fail.log: The yard dog. Of course the yard dog. By the time you get away it is too late for the ford. (-5 health)

choices.text: It is too far, and it is snowing. You cannot

effects.log: You lie in your earth and listen to the snow. On the next market day there is a white pelt on the trader's pole, and the boys crowd round to look at it. You do not go to the market. You never go to that market again.

events.text: Years on. The trader is old, and his son carries the pole now, and the boys who set snares at the ford have sons who set snares at the ford. Fox pelts on the pole, red and red and red. Two for a white, still. You watch the market from the hill and think about White-Paw, one way or the other, every time you see that pole.

choices.text: Make sure no snare stands at that ford ever again

effects.log: Every snare at the ford, every autumn, chewed through or dragged into the stream. The boys say the ford is cursed. They are not wrong. It is cursed with you.

choices.text: Keep your own fur out of sight of that pole

effects.log: A red fox is a coin. You are careful never to be a coin. It is a lesson that will matter more, much later, when your fur is not red any more.

choices.text: Go to the ford and sit where it happened

effects.log: Snow on the reeds. Water under the ice. You think: a white coat is worth a whole autumn's work to a man, and the whole of a life to a fox. Somewhere in that sum is the whole of the world.

events.text: Once a year, at the end of autumn, a woman in a good quilted jacket comes up the hill road alone and sits on the stone by your mound. She smells of sesame oil and wood smoke and people, and under all that, faintly, of fox. "I am your mother's elder sister," she says, in the small sounds. "Banya. I have been somebody's wife in the next valley for a very long time. Do not look at my shadow."

choices.text: Look at her shadow

effects.log: In the low sun her shadow lies long on the grass, and behind it, six tails, fanned. She sighs. "Everybody looks," she says. "Your mother looked. You will be told not to look all your life, and you will always look."

choices.text: Ask about your mother

effects.log: "She stood up on the hill road and went," Banya says. "Somewhere. With a face. That is all I know, and all I will say, because it is hers." She pats your head with a hand that has the right number of fingers.

choices.text: Ask how a fox can be somebody's wife for so long

effects.log: "Carefully," she says, and laughs, and does not explain. "Every day of it carefully. You will see. Or you will not, which is also a way to live."

events.text: Banya again, a year older, which on her means nothing at all. "The thousand days," she says, as if continuing a conversation. "If a fox harms nobody for a thousand days, not one, heaven counts it. That is the first gate. Most foxes never get through it. I got to six hundred once." She looks at her hands. "There was a carter who insulted me."

choices.text: Ask what happened with the carter

effects.log: "Nothing," she says. "That is what I am telling you. Nothing happened, and I wanted it to. That counts too, in a thousand days. Wanting counts." You go to sleep thinking about how heaven counts wanting.

choices.text: Ask why she has not tried again

effects.log: "I have," she says. "Every year. Eleven times." She is quiet for a long time. "The twelfth time I will not tell anyone, and perhaps that will be the trick."

choices.text: Promise her you will get to a thousand

effects.log: She laughs till she has to hold the stone. "Do not promise me," she says. "Promise the moon. The moon writes things down."

events.text: "There is a second gate," Banya says. Her jacket is a new one this year, blue, with good buttons. "A hundred days in a house, as one of the house, and nobody sees you as you are. Not once. Then you wake up with no tails. Then you are a person." She is quiet. "I knew a fox who got to ninety-nine. On the last night the one who loved it looked. Just to see. Just once."

choices.text: Ask what that fox did

effects.log: "Nothing," Banya says. "It went back to the mountain and left the house everything it had. It did not take revenge. That is the part they always leave out of the story: it did not take revenge." She looks at you. You understand who the fox was.

choices.text: Ask why anyone would look, after ninety-nine days

effects.log: "Because they loved it," she says. "You cannot love something for ninety-nine days and not want to see it. That is the cruelty of the gate. Heaven is not cruel. It is only exact."

choices.text: Say you would rather stay a fox

effects.log: "Good," says Banya. "Stay a fox as long as you can bear it. It is a fine thing to be. It is just not enough, after six tails. Nothing is enough, after six tails."

events.text: Banya comes late this year, in the snow, in an old jacket. "The eldest of my house is dying," she says. "Sixty-odd years I have called that one mine. They never knew. They will die not knowing, and I will sit by the bed and hold a hand, and then I will have to leave, because I do not grow old, and someone will notice." She looks at the village lights. "Every face ends like this. Remember that before you take one."

choices.text: Sit against her in the snow

effects.log: She puts her hand on your back and leaves it there till the snow covers both of you. In the morning she is gone down the hill road. Next autumn she does not come. The autumn after, she does, in a new face, and does not explain.

choices.text: Ask her if it was worth it

effects.log: "Sixty-odd years of being somebody," she says. "Long years of rice in a bowl with a lid, and a name with a family in it. Yes. And it will break me. Both." She gets up. "That is what a face is. Both."

choices.text: Tell her you will go with her down to the next valley

effects.log: "No," she says, very gently. "You have no face yet, and this is not a story for a fox without one." She goes alone. You watch her shadow on the snow until the six tails are too small to count.

events.text: Every dusk, a student walks home from the village school along the hill road past your mound, with a bundle of books and lips moving: reciting. Every dusk the student slows down at the old graves, where the road is darkest, and recites louder. You lie in the long grass and listen to the classics going by, a little at a time, like a river.

choices.text: Follow along in the grass, listening

effects.log: A page a night. By the end of the autumn you have heard a whole book of the classics walk past you, and you know which lines the student always gets wrong. You find you want to tell them. You cannot. Not yet.

choices.text: Watch the student, not the words

effects.log: Tired, hungry, frightened of the graves, brave anyway. Breath that steams in the cold, warm and slow. You notice the breath. You do not know why you notice the breath. You stop noticing it, on purpose.

choices.text: Keep away from the road at dusk

effects.log: There is something in you that wants to walk beside the student on the darkest part of the road. You do not know what it is, and you do not like not knowing. You go to the marsh instead.

events.text: The village school's old teacher tells the students a story at the end of term, and it carries across the paddy to your mound on the still air: a student on a hill road, a beautiful stranger, a bead passed with a breath, a student growing pale. "Swallow it," the teacher says, "and look at the sky. That is what the old story says." The children shriek. You lie very still with the bead behind your teeth.

choices.text: Close your mouth tight on the bead

effects.log: You hold it so tight your jaw aches. The third rule. Never let your bead into another mouth. For the first time, you understand that the rule is not only to protect you.

choices.text: Listen to the end of the story

effects.log: The student swallows the bead, runs, trips, and sees the earth instead of the sky, and becomes a great geomancer, and never knows heaven. "That is why people know the earth and not heaven," the teacher says. You lie awake all night wondering what the fox knew.

choices.text: Bark once across the paddy, to scare them

effects.log: One fox bark at exactly the right moment. The children scream, the teacher laughs, and every student in that school walks home the long way for a month. You have done the hill road's students a kindness. You are almost sure.

events.text: The student of the hill road passes the county examination. The whole village hears, and the student walks home past your mound one last time with a red tassel in their hat and nothing to recite, and stops at the old graves, and bows to them. To the graves. Or to the long grass beside them. You are not sure which.

choices.text: Stand up in the grass and let them see you

effects.log: A fox on its feet in the grass, looking back. The student laughs, a short surprised laugh, and bows again, deeper, unmistakably to you. Then they go down the hill road to their life. You will look for that face on that road for a hundred years.

choices.text: Stay hidden, and wish them well in your own way

effects.log: You flick one small orange light into the air above the road, very high, where it might be a star. The student does not see it. The wish goes anyway.

events.text: A student on the hill road at dusk looks up at the old graves, and for a moment you are sure the student is looking for something, a stranger, a game with a bead, and is afraid of it, and is ready for it. Somewhere behind those eyes is an old soul that once swallowed a fox's bead and fell, and looked at the earth. You feel the bead behind your teeth go cold.

choices.text: Keep far away from this one

effects.log: You stay in the grass until the student has gone. Whatever fox it was, it lost its bead to a human who listened to a schoolmaster. You have no intention of being the second.

choices.text: Watch, and learn what such a person looks like

effects.log: Steady feet, a careful glance at every shadow, a hand that touches the bundle of books as if for courage. Nothing you could name. You will know that look again, you think, on a hill road in a hundred years.

events.text: On the darkest part of the hill road, in the grass, you find a single red-brown hair, long and fine, caught on a thistle. Not yours, not from any fox of this hill, though nearly. It smells of an old road and of a person who once said to a fox, gently, "I know," and gave the bead back. Someone, in another life, was kind to one of you.

choices.text: Leave the hair where it is

effects.log: It is not yours to take. It is a thank-you, left for somebody, and somebody will come for it. You go home thinking about a person who knew, and gave it back, and said so.

choices.text: Carry it home to the deepest room of your earth

effects.log: You put it with the other things a fox keeps. It is the lightest of them, and the one you take out to look at most.

events.text: At the entrance to the village stand two tall wooden posts with carved faces: great round eyes, bared teeth, tall hats, and painted words down the front that keep out sickness and spirits and things that come by night. Every time you cross the road between them, your fur stands up and your feet go cold, as if someone very large were looking at you.

choices.text: Sit in the road and look up at them

effects.log: They look down. Carved eyes, cracked paint, a bird's nest in one hat. Nothing happens, except that you feel very small and very seen. They let you pass. You are not sure they would let something with more tails pass.

choices.text: Go round through the paddies instead

effects.log: The long way, through the mud. It is the way the vixen who raised you always went. You never ask whether foxes cannot cross between the posts, or only should not. You suspect the answer matters.

choices.text: Leave a stone on the cairn at their feet, like the villagers do

effects.log: You nose a small stone onto the pile at the foot of the posts. The cold in your feet goes, a little. Courtesy, it seems, works on wood as well as people.

events.text: A storm has cracked one of the guardian posts in half, and the village has not yet carved a new one. The broken face lies in the ditch, staring at the sky. The other post stands alone, and that night something comes up the road from the south that is not a person and not a fox: a cold, a sickness, a shape like mist with a smell of fever.

choices.text: Stand in the road where the broken post stood

ok.log: You stand in the gap with every hair on end, and the mist comes to you, and stops, and goes round you, and back down the road it came. In the morning the village carves a new post. Nobody ever knows. The standing post knows.

fail.log: It goes through you like cold water through a sieve, and on into the village. You lie in the ditch beside the broken face, shaking with fever, for three days. The village has a bad winter, but not as bad as it might have been. (-10 health)

choices.text: Run and bark at the headman's gate until they wake

effects.log: They come out cursing, and see the broken post, and the elders look at each other. By dawn there are torches at the entrance and a new post half-carved. Sometimes a fox bark is just a fox bark. Sometimes it is a warning that nobody admits to having heard.

choices.text: Keep away. Sickness is not a fox's business

effects.log: You go back to the hill. The fever comes through the village that winter. You hear the coughing from the mound all through the long nights, and tell yourself it is the wind.

events.text: The base of your tail has itched all winter, a deep itch like a bone growing. You are very old for a fox. Field foxes do not live so long, and you have. The old foxes on the ridge look at you differently this spring, and the dogs in the village, all of them, will not stop looking at your shadow.

choices.text: Hide the itch, the way she hid hers

effects.log: You walk carefully, sit carefully, keep your back to the lamps. Every tail is one more thing to hide. You have not even got it yet, and already you are hiding it.

choices.text: Sit on the mound every full moon until it comes

effects.log: You sit through every full moon of the spring with the itch like a fire at the root of your tail and the bead glowing behind your teeth. You are waiting for something. The moon is waiting too. (+2 Bead)

choices.text: Go and ask the old fox of the ridge what is happening

effects.log: "A hundred years," it says, without turning its head. "The second comes now, and then a face, and then you will never be only a fox again." It sounds sorry for you. It is the only kind thing it has ever said.

events.text: The hundredth spring. You go down to the paddies at dawn, the way you went as a kit with your littermates, and stop on the dyke over the flooded field. The water is still. In it, a red fox with a white chest looks up at you, and behind it, unmistakably, two tails.

choices.text: Look for a long time

effects.log: Two tails. One for the field fox you were, one for whatever you are now. You count them three times. Then you remember that you were told never to count, and laugh, a fox's laugh, which is mostly breath.

choices.text: Bow to the reflection, as to the moon

effects.log: You bow to the fox in the water, and it bows back. A hundred years of grave mounds, dogs, salt peddlers, moons. It has been a good first life. The second is about to begin.

choices.text: Splash the water and walk on

effects.log: The reflection breaks into a hundred pieces and every piece has two tails. You walk on along the dyke with your new tail held low, the way she held hers, and do not look back. You will be looking back for the rest of your life.

events.text: A yard dog you do not know, a new one, on the lane you always take to the paddies. It has smelled you. It is standing in its gate with its hackles up, and it has not barked yet, and you are both waiting to see which of you will move first.

choices.text: Go back the way you came, and find another lane

effects.log: Once is a fox. You make sure it is only once. That lane is closed to you now, until the dog is old. You are good at waiting for dogs to be old.

choices.text: Walk past it, slow and calm

ok.log: You walk past as if you belonged there. The dog, baffled, does not bark. It will dream about you for a week.

fail.log: It barks, and every dog in the village answers, and you are over three walls before the first lamp is lit. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lead it off on a chase, and lose it in the marsh

effects.log: It follows you into the reeds and comes out an hour later, alone, wet and confused. Its master beats the reeds with a stick and finds a heron. The village laughs for days.

events.text: A salt peddler on the hill road at dusk: not the one you know, a younger one, with a newer A-frame and the same forked stick. He is walking slowly, and looking at the verges, the long grass, the shadows. He is not looking for anything. He is just looking.

choices.text: Go flat in the grass until he is gone

effects.log: He passes within a body's length. He does not stop. Nobody has ever needed to tell you the second rule twice.

choices.text: Go the long way round, through the graves

effects.log: You go round by the old mounds and the cold breath, and come out on the far side of the hill. He is still walking. Salt peddlers are always still walking.

choices.text: Watch his stick

effects.log: He leans on it, props his frame on it, scratches his back with it. It is only a stick. It is the most frightening thing in the province.

events.text: A full moon, and a cold clear night, and the whole village is out on the threshing floor for a festival: drums, rice cakes, children running. From the mound you can see it all, small and bright, like something under glass. The moon pulls at the bead behind your teeth. The village pulls at something else.

choices.text: Bow to the moon all night

effects.log: You turn your back on the drums and bow to the moon. The bead grows a shade warmer. The drums go on without you. They always will. (+2 Bead)

choices.text: Creep down to the edge of the threshing floor and watch

effects.log: From the shadow of a straw stack you watch them dance, badly and happily. A child sees you and says nothing, and puts a rice cake on the ground by the stack. People. You will never understand them. You will never stop trying.
